A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same virtual-correspondence framework for three-camera relative pose estimation. All 19 pages of v2 and 22 pages of v3, including supplementary text, equations, figures, and tables, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic and real-data experiments, including PhotoTourism and KITTI comparisons, noise and outlier analyses, and supplementary two-view results.

after.justification: v3 reports original pose-estimation results on PhotoTourism and Cambridge Landmarks, alongside synthetic experiments, ablations, and supplementary comparisons.

M1.justification: v3 adds fourth-point hypothesis filtering (+F) and Levenberg–Marquardt refinement on the original four correspondences (+R), with calibrated and partially calibrated variants. These modify the solver procedure beyond v2's existing RANSAC local optimization. The underlying virtual-correspondence construction, neural architecture, and training loss remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 expands PhotoTourism evaluation beyond v2's two principal scenes and expands Cambridge Landmarks from the Shop Facade correspondence analysis to five-scene calibrated and shared-focal-length evaluation. KITTI driving-scene evaluation disappears. Synthetic training and ETH3D noise experiments remain; two-view estimation was already evaluated in v2.

E2.justification: v2's real-data comparisons include consecutive and joint 5pt/6pt estimation baselines, which v3 omits from the corresponding real-data comparisons. The joint 5PC comparator survives in the noise experiments. HC, 5pt/6pt+P3P, and oracle families remain. Newly cited GPU homotopy methods are explicitly not evaluated.

E3.justification: Real-data matching changes from RootSIFT with nearest-neighbor matching to SuperPoint/LightGlue, and evaluation adds PoseLib alongside GC-RANSAC. v3 selects δ=0.04 and refinement iterations using held-out St. Peter's Square, replacing v2's reported 0.15/0.1 shifts. It adds runtime-based evaluation and an all-camera-pairs error metric. Calibrated-solver timing sample counts change from 1,000 to over 10,000 instances, without establishing that those timings were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds refinement/filtering comparisons, an LM-iteration ablation, alternative-metric validation, and raw 4pt(M)-versus-5pt pose-accuracy analysis. Mean-point analysis now examines pose errors and recovered inliers as well as epipolar error. The δ and outlier studies are substantially revised, including runtime-based robustness comparisons; the earlier noise experiments remain.

E5.justification: v3 Table 1 newly reports ± quantities alongside mean errors and adds 20th-percentile summaries. The meaning of the ± quantities is not explicitly defined. Existing noise boxplots and their quantile conventions remain, and neither version documents seed-based confidence intervals or repeated-run significance testing.

E6.justification: Many results are added or replaced. v2 Table 2 reports KITTI AUC@5 of 72.05 for 4p3vf(M±0.15) versus 71.73 for 6pt+P3P; v3 Table 3 reports Cambridge values of 33.18 versus 38.44 for the corresponding solver families. These different settings do not establish a same-setting performance decline. v3 also adds +R/+F results and revised oracle rankings. v2's two-view Table 6 survives unchanged as v3 Table 4.

T1.justification: v3 Section 9.3 introduces a different mathematical definition of pose error: the maximum of rotation and translation errors across all three camera pairs. This supplements the retained metric based on averages for pairs 1–2 and 1–3. Lemma 1, its geometric proof, and the Sampson-loss expression are retained; configuration renotation is equivalent.

C1.justification: v2 presents mean-point and learned solvers as two principal contributions and describes 4p3vf as previously unsolved. v3 centers refined mean-point solvers, characterizes learning results as preliminary with negligible gains after refinement, and positions its focal-length solutions as efficient alternatives to existing homotopy methods.

C2.justification: v3 adds concrete explanations of low-overlap failures, small-triangle instability, and why an additional real correspondence can make 5pt+P3P more robust. It explains filtering's accuracy cost and refinement's reduction of the learning advantage. Its appendix attributes the revised oracle ranking to RANSAC termination behavior, although the main text retains the earlier contrary statement.

D1.justification: v3 documents a substantially revised experimental recipe, including a 2,048-feature cap, Cambridge resizing to 800 pixels, triplet eligibility requirements, PoseLib's 0.9999 stopping confidence, and hardware for runtime comparisons. v2's explicit C++/Eigen and default HC-implementation disclosures are omitted. The detailed network training recipe remains, and both versions still promise a future code release.

R1.justification: v3 adds existing 4p3vf homotopy solutions by Chien et al. and Dal Cin et al., materially changing the positioning from solving a previously unsolved problem to providing faster practical solutions. It also adds citations for SuperPoint, LightGlue, PoseLib, PointNet, and uncertainty propagation while trimming background references.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statements, method motivation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Network details move into the supplement, the separate discussion is integrated into experiments, and supplementary sections are reorganized around mean-point analysis, learning, and validation. References move after the supplement, and the author list expands.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, and v3 adds multi-metric heatmaps, refinement plots, and extensive AUC-versus-runtime panels. Real-data tables are restructured around datasets and solver variants, while individual timings become standalone tables. Earlier mean-point heatmaps, network diagrams, and noise plots are relocated. v3 Tables 6 and 8 duplicate the alternative-metric results.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens practical validation through broader scene testing in two RANSAC frameworks, held-out parameter selection, refinement ablations, measured speed–accuracy trade-offs, and evaluation of all three camera pairs. It also clarifies failure conditions and qualifies the learning contribution. Removing KITTI and some real-data baselines reduces coverage, and the inconsistent oracle statements remain a reporting weakness, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and interpretability.
